note: Wren Phonics — Handwriting guide (b410, 2026-10-08), built from the DfE's SSP validation criteria (supporting documentation, Note 3) and criterion C11, in Wren's own words. provenance: Wren original, b410, 2026-10-08.
intro: Letter formation is taught print only (no cursive, no joining or lead-in strokes) at this stage, matching every piece of text children are given to read — the DfE's SSP validation criteria (supporting documentation, Note 3) are explicit that joining strokes are not taught yet because they add difficulty without yet adding value.
exit_stroke_rule: A simple exit stroke — a small flick to the right at the end of the letter — is allowed, once the plain shape is secure, for these ten lowercase letters only: a, d, h, i, k, l, m, n, t, u (Note 3, footnote 3). No other lowercase letter, and no capital letter, carries an exit stroke at this stage; it is not taught as part of learning the shape, only added later once the shape itself is confident.
sequence_rationale_reception: Lowercase letters are practised in the SAME order their sound is taught in the main phonics schedule, not a separate alphabetical or family-grouped order — a child forms the shape of a letter in the same week they learn what it sounds like, so the two reinforce each other. "q" has no sound of its own in this programme (it is always taught as "qu") but still needs its own formation practice, placed at the point "qu" is taught.
reception_capitals_note: Capitals are not left until Year 1 across the board — three uses are taught in Reception as soon as they are needed: writing "I" (a tricky word from Reception Autumn 2), writing the first letter of your own name, and starting a sentence once the writing progression below reaches that stage. The Year 1 sequence below is for every OTHER capital letter, practised systematically once lowercase formation is secure.
sequence_rationale_year1: The remaining capital letters are not tied to the phonics schedule the same way — they are introduced once lowercase formation across the alphabet is secure, grouped by family so similar movements are practised together rather than jumping between very different shapes from one day to the next.
writing_progression: Writing moves through three stages, in order, never skipped: forming single graphemes correctly -> writing whole words made only of already-taught GPCs -> writing simple sentences using taught GPCs and taught tricky words. A child is never asked to write independently with sounds or words they have not yet been taught (DfE criterion C11).
